Public Prosecutor, High Court Of Kerala

entities.label: RESPONDENT

sentences.text:
The first and second accused in C.C.No.539 of 2003 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Nadapuram, filed this revision petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 16 (1) (a) (i), 7 (i) and 2 (ia)
(a)
(m) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 r/w Rule 5 Appendix B.A.16.06 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955.
2.

entities.text: Judicial Magistrate of First Class, Nadapuram
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: Heard.

3. The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 23.04.2003 at about 11 a.m., PW1, the Food Inspector purchased 3 bottles of tomato sauce, each bottle contained 200 gram from the first accused.
The second accused was the licensee of the shop and the third accused was the manufacturer.
After sampling as per rules, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis.

The public analyst submitted Ext.P14 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for tomato sauce as per the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and was therefore adulterated.
Thereafter, on the request of the accused, the second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis.

Ext.P28 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory would also show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for tomato sauce as per the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules and was therefore adulterated.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW5 were examined and Exts.P1 to P35 were marked for the prosecution.
DW1 was examined for the revision petitioners.

Abdulla K.K vs Food Inspector on 14 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/163813017/
2 5.

The learned counsel for the revision petitioners has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext.P28 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioners relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee)
and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext.P28 certificate of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra)
that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioners and the learned Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the decision in Pepsico India Holdings (supra), the conviction in this case cannot be sustained as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

In the result, this revision petition stands allowed setting aside the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 16 (1) (a) (i), 7 (i) and 2 (ia) (a) (m) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 r/w Rule 5 Appendix B.A.16.06 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules,
1955 and the revision petitioners are acquitted for the said offence.
The bail bonds of the revision petitioners stand cancelled and they are set at liberty.
B. SUDHEENDRA KUMAR JUDGE Scl/14.03.2016.
